plan: In a second-price sealed-bid auction, bidding one's true value is a dominant strategy: it guarantees winning whenever the value exceeds the second-highest bid (positive profit) and avoids overpaying since the price paid is determined by the second-highest bid, not my own bid. Bidding higher than value risks winning at a loss; bidding lower risks losing profitable opportunities. Given my value of $25, the optimal action is to bid exactly $25, ensuring truthful revelation and maximizing expected profit regardless of competitors' strategies.

In a second-price auction, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy: you win whenever your value exceeds the second-highest bid, and you pay that second-highest bid regardless of your own bid (as long as you're highest). Bidding above value risks paying more than the item is worth; bidding below value risks losing profitable opportunities. With no prior round history to adjust for, I'll bid exactly my private value of $17 to guarantee optimal expected profit this round.

In a second-price sealed-bid auction, bidding your true value is a dominant strategy regardless of the number of competitors. This holds because you pay the second-highest bid, not your own bid, so there's no incentive to shade your bid up or down—overbidding risks losing money if you win, and underbidding risks losing profitable wins. With my value at $39, I should bid exactly $39 to maximize expected profit.
